{{Short description|Economical computational problem}}
'''Nash equilibrium (NE) computation''' is a class of [[computational problem]]s in the intersection of [[game theory]] and [[computer science]]. The input to this problem is a [[normal-form game]], usually represented as a list of payoff matrices. The required output is a [[Nash equilibrium]] of the game.

NE computation can be broadly divided into computing [[Mixed Strategy|mixed-strategy]] NE vs computing [[Pure strategy|pure-strategy]] NE.  In each of these cases, one can consider computing an exact NE or an ''[[Epsilon-equilibrium|epsilon-approximate NE]]:''

* In an exact NE, no player can gain by deviating;
* In an epsilon-approximate NE, no player can gain more than epsilon by deviating. The utilities are normalized to [0,1], so this is actually a multiplicative approximation: the gain cannot be more than epsilon times the highest utility.
The special case of NE computation in two-player [[zero-sum game]]s is known as [[min-max optimization]]. The present page studies the more general problem of non-zero-sum games with many players.

== Mixed-strategy equilibria ==
When mixed strategies are allowed, every game has a Nash equilibrium. This was proved by [[John Forbes Nash Jr.|John Nash]] in 1950<ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last1=Nash |first1=John F. |year=1950 |title=Equilibrium points in n-person games |journal=PNAS |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=48–49 |bibcode=1950PNAS...36...48N |doi=10.1073/pnas.36.1.48 |pmc=1063129 |pmid=16588946 |doi-access=free}}</ref> using the [[Kakutani fixed-point theorem]], and later in 1951<ref name=":9">{{cite journal |last=Nash |first=John |date=1951 |title=Non-Cooperative Games |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=286–295 |doi=10.2307/1969529 |jstor=1969529}}</ref> using the [[Brouwer fixed-point theorem]]. For games with a small number of actions per player, a NE can be computed manually by solving a set of equations. However, when the number of actions per player grows, the number of possible strategy vectors grows exponentially, and the computation becomes computationally hard.

=== Non-polynomial-time algorithms ===
There are various algorithms that work well in practice, but do not guarantee termination in polynomial time. One of the most famous such algorithms is the [[Lemke–Howson algorithm]].<ref name="lh">{{cite journal |last1=Lemke |first1=C. E. |last2=Howson |first2=J. T. |year=1964 |title=Equilibrium points of bimatrix games |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=413–423 |doi=10.1137/0112033 |author-link1=Carlton E. Lemke}}</ref>

Porter, Nudelman and Shoham<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Porter |first1=Ryan |last2=Nudelman |first2=Eugene |last3=Shoham |first3=Yoav |date=2008-07-01 |title=Simple search methods for finding a Nash equilibrium |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825606000935 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |series=Second World Congress of the Game Theory Society |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=642–662 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2006.03.015 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> present an algorithm based on simple search heuristics, that performs well in practice on a large variety of games. They use the GAMUT testbed for testing the performance of their algorithm.

Lipton, Markakis and Mehta<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Lipton |first1=Richard J. |last2=Markakis |first2=Evangelos |last3=Mehta |first3=Aranyak |chapter=Playing large games using simple strategies |date=2003-06-09 |title=Proceedings of the 4th ACM conference on Electronic commerce |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/779928.779933 |series=EC '03 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=36–41 |doi=10.1145/779928.779933 |isbn=978-1-58113-679-1}}</ref> presented a [[Quasi-polynomial time]] algorithm for computing an approximate NE. It takes time <math>n^{\log n}</math>, where ''n'' is the number of possible actions per player.  They do it by proving the existence of an approximate NE strategies with support logarithmic in ''n,'' and proving that the payoffs to all players in any exact NE can be ε-approximated by such an approximate NE. They also prove that, if the payoff matrices have constant rank, then an exact NE can be found in polytime.

=== Computational hardness ===
Daskalakis, Goldberg and Papadimitriou<ref name="DGP2009">[https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/1461928.1461951 Constantinos Daskalakis, Paul W. Goldberg, and Christos H. Papadimitriou (2009). "The complexity of computing a Nash equilibrium."]</ref> proved that finding a NE is [[PPAD (complexity)|PPAD-complete]] in games with four or more players; later, Chen and Deng<ref name="ChenDeng2006">[[Xi Chen]] and [[Xiaotie Deng]] (2006),[https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1109/FOCS.2006.69. "Settling the complexity of two-player Nash equilibrium."] ''47th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 2006)'', 261–272.</ref> extended the result even for two-player games ([[bimatrix game]]s). Under standard complexity assumptions, these hardness results imply that no polynomial-time algorithm is expected for general equilibrium computation.

Computing a Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete even for ''win-lose bimatrix games'', that is, two-player games in which the payoff of each player is either 0 or 1.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

Etessami and Yannakkis<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Etessami |first1=Kousha |last2=Yannakakis |first2=Mihalis |date=January 2010 |title=On the Complexity of Nash Equilibria and Other Fixed Points |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/080720826 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=39 |issue=6 |pages=2531–2597 |doi=10.1137/080720826 |issn=0097-5397|hdl=20.500.11820/98752471-0a7a-4366-8871-b8f1984190ef |hdl-access=free }}</ref> (who defined the complexity class [[FIXP (complexity)|FIXP]]) proved that computing an exact or approximate NE for 3 or more players is FIXP-complete. They also show that computing an approximate NE with any approximation factor smaller than 1/2 is at least as hard as the [[square-root sum problem]], as well as a more general arithmetic circuit decision problem.

=== Approximation algorithms ===
Tsaknakis and Spirakis<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Tsaknakis |first1=Haralampos |last2=Spirakis |first2=Paul G. |chapter=An Optimization Approach for Approximate Nash Equilibria |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2007 |volume=4858 |editor-last=Deng |editor-first=Xiaotie |editor2-last=Graham |editor2-first=Fan Chung |title=Internet and Network Economics |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-77105-0_8 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=42–56 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-77105-0_8 |isbn=978-3-540-77105-0|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> presented a polytime algorithm that finds an 0.3393-approximate NE for a bimatrix game (that is, the gain from deviation cannot be more than 0.3393 times the maximum utility). Their algorithm minimizes a certain function, representing the distance from NE, using [[gradient descent]]. The procedure converges in polynomial time to local optima which are 0.3393-approximate NE.

Deligkas, Fearnley, Savani and Spirakis<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deligkas |first1=Argyrios |last2=Fearnley |first2=John |last3=Savani |first3=Rahul |last4=Spirakis |first4=Paul |date=2017-02-01 |title=Computing Approximate Nash Equilibria in Polymatrix Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-015-0078-7 |journal=Algorithmica |volume=77 |issue=2 |pages=487–514 |doi=10.1007/s00453-015-0078-7 |issn=1432-0541|url-access=subscription }}</ref> extend the descent techniques to [[polymatrix game]]s, attaining an (0.5+δ)-approximate NE in time polynomial in the input size and 1/δ. For general ''n''-player games, the approximation ratio increases with ''n'' (e.g. it is 0.6022 for n=3 and 0.7153 for n=4).

=== Approximation hardness ===
The PPAD-completeness results in <ref name="DGP2009" /><ref name="ChenDeng2006" /> in fact show that computing an ε-approximate NE is PPAD-complete, if ε is exponentially small (smaller than 2<sup>-m</sup>, where m is the number of actions per player).

Chen Deng and Teng<ref name=":10" /> proved PPAD-hardness even for ε that is polynomially small. In other words, they proved that no algorithm with runtime polynomial in n and 1/ε can compute an ε-approximate Nash equilibrium in a two-player game with ''n'' actions per player, unless [[PPAD (complexity)|PPAD]] ≤ P. In particular, this means that there is probably no [[FPTAS]] for NE.

Aviad Rubinstein<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rubinstein |first=Aviad |chapter=Inapproximability of Nash Equilibrium |date=2015-06-14 |title=Proceedings of the forty-seventh annual ACM symposium on Theory of Computing |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2746539.2746578 |series=STOC '15 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=409–418 |doi=10.1145/2746539.2746578 |arxiv=1405.3322 |isbn=978-1-4503-3536-2}}</ref> showed that finding an ε-approximate Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete even for a simple class of games: [[Graphical game (game theory)|graphical games]] of degree three, in which each agent has only two actions; and even when ε is a constant. In particular, there is no [[Polynomial-time approximation scheme|PTAS]] for NE in general games (He also proved inapproximability for other related problems, such as: [[Bayesian Nash equilibrium]] in a two-player game, relative ε-Nash equilibrium in a two-player game, [[market equilibrium]] in a non-monotone market as well as [[Approximate Competitive Equilibrium from Equal Incomes|approximate competitive equilibrium from equal incomes]]).

Later, Rubinstein<ref>{{Citation |last=Rubinstein |first=Aviad |title=Settling the complexity of computing approximate two-player Nash equilibria |date=2016-08-29 |arxiv=1606.04550 }}</ref> proved that, assuming the [[Exponential time hypothesis]] for PPAD, there exists a positive constant ε such that computing ε-approximate NE in a two-player game with ''n'' actions per player requires [[quasi-polynomial time]], as in the <ref name=":0" /> algorithm.

=== Smoothed complexity ===
[[Smoothed analysis]] has been used to prove that many problems that are computationally-hard in the worst case, are in fact "almost always" easy, that is, if a problem is perturbed randomly, then the perturbed problem is easy. Interestingly, this is ''not'' the case for the problem of computing a NE. In particular:

* Chen, Deng and Teng<ref name=":10">{{Cite book |last1=Chen |first1=Xi |last2=Deng |first2=Xiaotie |last3=Teng |first3=Shang-hua |chapter=Computing Nash Equilibria: Approximation and Smoothed Complexity |date=October 2006 |title=2006 47th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS'06) |pages=603–612 |doi=10.1109/FOCS.2006.20 |arxiv=cs/0602043 |isbn=0-7695-2720-5 }}</ref> proved that no algorithm for computing NE in a two-player game has smoothed complexity polynomial in ''n'' and 1/''s'', where ''s'' is the input perturbation size, unless PPAD ≤ [[RP (complexity)|RP]]. In particular, the smoothed complexity of the [[Lemke-Howson]] algorithm is probably not polynomial.
* Boodaghians, Brakensiek, Hopkins and Rubinstein<ref>{{Citation |last1=Boodaghians |first1=Shant |title=Smoothed Complexity of 2-player Nash Equilibria |date=2020-07-21 |arxiv=2007.10857 |last2=Brakensiek |first2=Joshua |last3=Hopkins |first3=Samuel B. |last4=Rubinstein |first4=Aviad}}</ref> prove that computing NE in a 2-player game is PPAD-hard (under randomized reductions) even when smoothing with noise of constant magnitude.

=== Irrationality of outcomes ===
All  two-player games with rational payoff matrices always have only NE with rational probabilities. However, there are three-player games with rational payoff matrices, in which every NE requires [[Irrationality|irrational]] probabilities, which cannot be output accurately in finite time. An example was already shown by Nash<ref name=":9" />{{Reference page|page=293}}: it is a simplified variant of [[Poker]] for three players, with a unique NE in which all probabilities are linear functions of sqrt(321), which is an [[irrational number]]. Another example can be found in <ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Bilò |first1=Vittorio |last2=Mavronicolas |first2=Marios |date=2014-04-01 |title=Complexity of Rational and Irrational Nash Equilibria |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00224-013-9523-7 |journal=Theory of Computing Systems |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=491–527 |doi=10.1007/s00224-013-9523-7 |issn=1433-0490|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Proposition 3}}: it is a three-player game where each player has only two possible actions "0" and "1". There is a unique NE in which all players choose "0" with probabilities that are linear functions of sqrt(409).

Datta<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Datta |first=Ruchira S. |date=August 2003 |title=Universality of Nash Equilibria |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/moor.28.3.424.16397 |journal=Mathematics of Operations Research |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=424–432 |doi=10.1287/moor.28.3.424.16397 |arxiv=math/0301001 |issn=0364-765X}}</ref> shows that every real [[algebraic variety]] is isomorphic to the set of totally mixed Nash equilibria of some three-person game, and also to the set of totally mixed Nash equilibria of an ''n''-person game in which each player has two actions. This means that, in each of these classes, there are games whose probabilities require roots of any real polynomial.{{Clarify|date=July 2025}}

Orzech and Rinard<ref>{{Citation |last1=Orzech |first1=Edan |title=Nash Equilibria with Irradical Probabilities |date=2025-07-12 |arxiv=2507.09422 |last2=Rinard |first2=Martin}}</ref> show that, for any n ≥ 4, there is an n-player game where all payoffs are in {0,1,2}, with a unique NE in which all the probabilities are [[irradical number]]s ([[algebraic number]]s that cannot be expressed with ''m''-th roots for any integer ''m'').

=== Two-Player Zero-Sum Games ===
Two-player [[zero-sum game]]s represent the most fundamental class with polynomial-time equilibrium computation. In these games, one player's gain equals the other's loss, creating a pure conflict scenario. The key insight is that NE in zero-sum games correspond to minimax strategies, which can be computed via [[linear programming]]. For a zero-sum game with payoff matrix ''A'' for the row player, the [[minimax theorem]] of [[John von Neumann]] establishes that the game value can be computed by solving [[dual linear program]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=von Neumann |first=John |date=1928 |title=Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele |journal=Mathematische Annalen |volume=100 |issue=1 |pages=295–320 |doi=10.1007/BF01448847}}</ref> Since linear programming can be solved in polynomial time using [[interior-point method]]s or the [[ellipsoid algorithm]], NE can be computed in time polynomial in the size of the payoff matrices.

=== Anonymous games ===
In an [[anonymous game]], the payoff of each player depends only on his own strategy and on the ''number'' of players taking every strategy, but not on their identity. Anonymous games admit efficient computation of approximate NE. In particular:

* Daskalakis and Papadimitriou<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last1=Daskalakis |first1=Constantinos |last2=Papadimitriou |first2=Christos |chapter=Computing Equilibria in Anonymous Games |date=October 2007 |title=48th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS'07) |pages=83–93 |doi=10.1109/FOCS.2007.24 |arxiv=0710.5582 |isbn=978-0-7695-3010-9 }}</ref> presented polytime approximation algorithms for games with many players but few strategies (''s'' strategies per player). Their algorithm computes a <math>s^2L</math>-approximate pure NE, where ''L'' is the [[Lipschitz constant]] of the utility functions. They also show a [[Polynomial-time approximation scheme|PTAS]] for mixed NE when ''s''=2. In a later work,<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Daskalakis |first1=Constantinos |last2=Papadimitriou |first2=Christos H. |date=2015-03-01 |title=Approximate Nash equilibria in anonymous games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022053114000209 |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |series=Computer Science and Economic Theory |volume=156 |pages=207–245 |doi=10.1016/j.jet.2014.02.002 |issn=0022-0531|url-access=subscription }}</ref> they prove that approximate mixed NE in anonymous games can be computed in polytime to any desired accuracy, if the number of strategies is a constant (i.e., there is a PTAS). Moreover, if the utility functions are [[Lipschitz continuous]], one can compute in polytime an approximate pure NE, whose quality depends on the number of strategies and the Lipschitz constant. If the game has two strategies, there always exists an approximate NE in which either only a small number of players randomize, or of those who do, they all randomize the same way.
* Cheng, Diakonikolas and Stewart<ref>{{Citation |last1=Cheng |first1=Yu |chapter=Playing Anonymous Games using Simple Strategies |date=January 2017 |title=Proceedings of the 2017 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) |pages=616–631 |chapter-url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611974782.40 |access-date=2025-07-29 |series=Proceedings |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |doi=10.1137/1.9781611974782.40 |last2=Diakonikolas |first2=Ilias |last3=Stewart |first3=Alistair |isbn=978-1-61197-478-2 |arxiv=1608.07336 }}</ref> present other algorithms for finding approximate mixed NE in anonymous games, where the strategies of the players are "simple": each player plays one strategy with probability 1—δ, for some small δ, and plays uniformly at random with probability ''δ.''
* In contrast, Chen Durfee and Orfanou<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chen |first1=Xi |last2=Durfee |first2=David |last3=Orfanou |first3=Anthi |chapter=On the Complexity of Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games |date=2015-06-14 |title=Proceedings of the forty-seventh annual ACM symposium on Theory of Computing |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2746539.2746571 |series=STOC '15 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=381–390 |doi=10.1145/2746539.2746571 |isbn=978-1-4503-3536-2}}</ref> prove that, if the approximation parameter is exponentially small in the number of players, then the problem is [[PPAD-complete]] when there are at least 7 strategies.

=== Graphical Games ===
'''[[Graphical game (game theory)|Graphical games]]''' represent strategic interactions using graphs where each player's payoff depends only on neighbors' actions, enabling algorithms that exploit sparsity.

In general, computing NE on graphical games is still PPAD-hard, even if the graph degree is at most 3 and each player has only 2 actions.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last1=Elkind |first1=Edith |last2=Goldberg |first2=Leslie Ann |last3=Goldberg |first3=Paul |chapter=Nash equilibria in graphical games on trees revisited |date=2006-06-11 |title=Proceedings of the 7th ACM conference on Electronic commerce |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1134707.1134719 |series=EC '06 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=100–109 |doi=10.1145/1134707.1134719 |isbn=978-1-59593-236-5}}</ref> However, when the graph is a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] with a bounded degree, more efficient algorithms are possible.

Kearns, Littman and Singh<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kearns |first1=Michael |last2=Littman |first2=Michael L. |last3=Singh |first3=Satinder |date=2001 |title=Graphical models for game theory |journal=Proceedings of the Seventeenth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence |pages=253–260 |arxiv=1301.2281 }}</ref> presented a [[dynamic programming]] algorithm for computing ''all'' NE of a tree-graphical game (with two actions per player); its run-time is exponential, but it allows to compute approximate NE in polynomial time. The algorithm requires only messages between neighboring nodes, and thus can be implemented in a [[Distributed algorithm|distributed]] fashion.

They then proposed a modification that can find a single NE in polytime. However, Elkind, Goldberg and Goldberg<ref name=":7" /> showed that the modification is incorrect (does not always find a NE). Based on their ideas, they proposed a new algorithm that computes all NE in quadratic time for a [[Path (graph theory)|path graph]], and in polynomial time for a general graph of degree at most 2. For general trees, the run-time of this algorithm is exponential even when the tree has bounded degree and its [[pathwidth]] is 2, but the same is true for  any algorithm of the same kind. Finding a NE for a degree-3 graphical game with constant pathwidth and 2 actions per player is PPAD-complete.

Bramoulle, Kranton and D'Amours<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bramoullé |first1=Yann |last2=Kranton |first2=Rachel |last3=D'Amours |first3=Martin |date=March 2014 |title=Strategic Interaction and Networks |url=https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.104.3.898 |journal=American Economic Review |volume=104 |issue=3 |pages=898–930 |doi=10.1257/aer.104.3.898 |issn=0002-8282}}</ref> study graphical games in which the best response function of each player is a [[Linear form|linear function]] of the actions of his neighbors. They prove that the Nash equilibrium depends only on a single parameter of the graph: the smallest [[eigenvalue]] of the matrix representing the graph. Hence, it can be computed efficiently.{{Clarify|date=July 2025}}

=== Win-Lose Games ===
'''Win-lose games''' are games in which all payoffs are either 0 or 1.

* Codenotti, Leoncini and Resta<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Codenotti |first1=Bruno |title=Algorithms – ESA 2006 |last2=Leoncini |first2=Mauro |last3=Resta |first3=Giovanni |date=2006 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-38876-0 |editor-last=Azar |editor-first=Yossi |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4168 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |pages=232–243 |chapter=Efficient Computation of Nash Equilibria for Very Sparse Win-Lose Bimatrix Games |doi=10.1007/11841036_23 |hdl=11380/641688 |editor2-last=Erlebach |editor2-first=Thomas |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11841036_23}}</ref> presented a linear-time algorithm for win-lose ''bimatrix'' games where the number of winning positions per strategy of each of the players is at most two. 
* Liu, Li and Deng<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zhengyang |last2=Li |first2=Jiawei |last3=Deng |first3=Xiaotie |date=2021-05-18 |title=On the Approximation of Nash Equilibria in Sparse Win-Lose Multi-player Games |url=https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/16699 |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |volume=35 |issue=6 |pages=5557–5565 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v35i6.16699 |issn=2374-3468|doi-access=free }}</ref> showed that, for [[Succinct game|''polymatrix'' games]], approximating a Nash equilibrium with polynomial precision is PPAD-hard, even for sparse win-lose games.

=== Bounded-rank bimatrix games ===
'''Rank-1 bimatrix games''' have payoff matrices that can be written as outer products of vectors. Adsul, Garg, Mehta and Sohoni<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Adsul |first1=Bharat |title=Proceedings of the forty-third annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing |last2=Garg |first2=Jugal |last3=Mehta |first3=Ruta |last4=Sohoni |first4=Milind |date=2011-06-06 |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |isbn=978-1-4503-0691-1 |series=STOC '11 |location=New York, NY, USA |pages=195–204 |chapter=Rank-1 bimatrix games: A homeomorphism and a polynomial time algorithm |doi=10.1145/1993636.1993664 |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1993636.1993664}}</ref> presented a polytime algorithm for exact NE. They also presented an algorithm to enumerate all the NE of a rank-1 game.\

'''Bounded rank bimatrix games''': Lipton, Markakis and Mehta<ref name=":0" /> prove that, for two players, if the payoff matrices have constant rank, then an exact NE can be found in polytime.

=== Auction Games ===
Auctions with dominant strategies (e.g. [[second-price auction]] and some special cases of [[combinatorial auction]]s<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lehmann |first1=Daniel |last2=O'Callaghan |first2=Liadan |last3=Shoham |first3=Yoav |date=2002 |title=Truth revelation in approximately efficient combinatorial auctions |journal=Journal of the ACM |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=577–602 |doi=10.1145/585265.585266}}</ref>) clearly have pure-strategy NE that can be computed efficiently. But even for [[First-price sealed-bid auction|first-price auctions]], which do not have dominant strategies, it is often possible to compute NE directly, by direct computation using knowledge of agents' distributions. For example,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Krishna |first=Vijay |title=Auction Theory |date=2009 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0123745071}}</ref> when all ''n'' buyers  have uniform valuations on [0,1], the equilibrium bidding function is: ''b''(''v'') = (''n''-1)''v''/''n.''

== Pure-strategy equilibria ==
A pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (PNE) is not guaranteed to exist in general games, though there are special classes of games in which a PNE always exists.

=== Deciding existence ===
Gottlob, Greco and Sarcello<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Gottlob |first1=Georg |last2=Greco |first2=Gianluigi |last3=Scarcello |first3=Francesco |date=2005-09-01 |title=Pure Nash equilibria: hard and easy games |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/1622519.1622530 |journal=J. Artif. Intell. Res. |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=357–406 |doi=10.1613/jair.1683  |doi-access=free|issn=1076-9757|arxiv=1109.2152 }}</ref> prove that, even in very restrictive settings, deciding the existence of a PNE is NP-hard. Deciding the existence of a [[strong Nash equilibrium]] is even harder: it is Σ<sup>''P''</sup><sub>2</sub>-complete.

However, when the utility function for each player depends only on the actions of a logarithmically small number of other players (that is, the dependency graph of the game has a small degree), then finding a PNE can be done in polytime. For graphical games, these problems are [[LOGCFL]]-complete.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Gottlob |first1=Georg |last2=Greco |first2=Gianluigi |last3=Scarcello |first3=Francesco |chapter=Pure Nash equilibria: Hard and easy games |date=2003-06-20 |title=Proceedings of the 9th conference on Theoretical aspects of rationality and knowledge |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/846241.846269 |series=TARK '03 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=215–230 |doi=10.1145/846241.846269 |isbn=978-1-58113-731-6}}</ref>

=== Anonymous games ===
Daskalakis and Papadimitriou<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> proved that [[anonymous game]]s with [[Lipschitz continuous]] utility functions and at most s strategies always contain an <math>s^2L</math>-approximate PNE, where ''L'' is the [[Lipschitz constant]] of the utility functions; such a PNE can compute in polytime.

=== Graphical games ===
Gottlob, Greco and Sarcello<ref name=":6" /> present algorithms for graphical games where the graphs with '''bounded [[treewidth]]'''. They show that a PNE can be found in polynomial time using tree decomposition techniques. The algorithm's complexity is exponential in the treewidth but polynomial in the game size.

=== Potential games and Congestion games ===
[[Potential game]]s always have a PNE. Potential games satisfy the '''Finite Improvement Property''': every sequence of unilateral beneficial deviations terminates at a Nash equilibrium.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Monderer |first1=Dov |last2=Shapley |first2=Lloyd S. |date=1996 |title=Potential Games |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=124–143 |doi=10.1006/game.1996.0044}}</ref> This immediately gives a simple algorithm: start with any strategy profile; while some player can improve their payoff by switching strategies - let that player switch to a better strategy; return the final strategy profile (guaranteed to be a Nash equilibrium). However, this algorithm might go through exponentially many different states before it converges.

Fabrikant, [[Christos Papadimitriou|Papadimitriou]] and Talwar<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last1=Fabrikant |first1=Alex |title=Proceedings of the thirty-sixth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing |last2=Papadimitriou |first2=Christos |last3=Talwar |first3=Kunal |date=2004-06-13 |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |isbn=978-1-58113-852-8 |series=STOC '04 |location=New York, NY, USA |pages=604–612 |chapter=The complexity of pure Nash equilibria |doi=10.1145/1007352.1007445 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1007352.1007445 |s2cid=1037326}}</ref> studied the special case of [[congestion game]]s (which are equivalent to ''exact'' potential games). They proved that:

* PNE can be found in polytime in the special case of ''symmetric network congestion games''. Such a game is represented by a directed graph with two nodes marked as "source" and "target". The set of actions available to each player is the set of paths from the source to the target. For each edge, there is a delay which is a function of the number of players who use it. The payoff to each player is minus the total delay on his chosen path. In this special case, a PNE can be computed in polynomial time by maximizing the potential, through reduction to [[Minimum-cost flow problem|min-cost flow]].
*In contrast, for ''asymmetric network congestion games'' (which are network congestion games in which each player has a different source and a different target), computing a PNE is [[PLS (complexity)|PLS-complete]]. The same holds for ''non-network congestion games'' (games in which all agents have the same set of strategies, but it is not the set of paths in any graph), whether symmetric or not. The proof implies that there are examples of such games in which some improvement paths are exponentially long. It also implies that the problem of finding a PNE reachable from a given input state is [[PSPACE-complete]].
* The class of ordinal potential games is even larger than the class of congestion games: every problem in the class [[PLS (complexity)|PLS]] can be presented as an ordinal potential game, where the set of PNE coincides with the set of local optima.
They also study the case of ''[[Non-atomic game|nonatomic]]'' congestion games. Computing a PNE in a nonatomic congestion game can be rephrased as a [[convex optimization]] problem, and thus can be approximated in wealky-polynomial time (e.g. by the [[ellipsoid method]]). Fabrikant, [[Christos Papadimitriou|Papadimitriou]] and Talwar<ref name=":14" /> presented a strongly-polytime algorithm for finding a PNE in the special case of nonatomic ''network'' congestion games. In this special case there is a graph ''G''; for each type ''i'' there are two nodes ''s<sub>i</sub>'' and ''t<sub>i</sub>'' from ''G''; and the set of strategies available to type ''i'' is the set of all paths from ''s<sub>i</sub>'' to ''t<sub>i</sub>''. If the utility functions of all players are [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]] with constant ''L'', then their algorithm computes an e-approximate PNE in [[strongly-polynomial time]] - polynomial in ''n'', ''L'' and 1/''e''.

Ackermann, Roglin and Vocking<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ackermann |first1=Heiner |last2=Röglin |first2=Heiko |last3=Vöcking |first3=Berthold |date=2008-12-17 |title=On the impact of combinatorial structure on congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1455248.1455249 |journal=J. ACM |volume=55 |issue=6 |pages=25:1–25:22 |doi=10.1145/1455248.1455249 |issn=0004-5411|url-access=subscription }}</ref> prove that, if the strategy space of each player consists of the [[Basis of a matroid|bases of a matroid]] over the set of resources, then all best-response sequences converge in polynomial number of steps, and the matroid property is essential for guaranteeing polynomial-time convergence. They also present a simpler technique for hardness proofs; using this technique, they prove that computing a PNE in (asymmetric) network congestion games is PLS-complete for directed and undirected networks, even if all delay functions are linear.

Chien and Sinclair<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chien |first1=Steve |last2=Sinclair |first2=Alistair |date=2011-03-01 |title=Convergence to approximate Nash equilibria in congestion games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825609001110 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |volume=71 |issue=2 |pages=315–327 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2009.05.004 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> study an "''ε''-greedy dynamics" in which, at each step, some player plays a move that decreases its cost by at least a factor of (1+''ε''). They prove that, in ''symmetric'' congestion games, when the delay functions satisfy some technical condition they call "bounded-jump", this ''ε''-greedy dynamics converges to an ''ε''-approximate PNE in a number of steps polynomial in the number of players and 1/''ε''. This result holds for various update policies and sequences, as long as they satisfy the weak condition that each player has an opportunity to play eventually. The result holds even when a constant number of resources have arbitrary cost functions.

Skopalik and Vocking<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Skopalik |first1=Alexander |last2=Vöcking |first2=Berthold |chapter=Inapproximability of pure nash equilibria |date=2008-05-17 |title=Proceedings of the fortieth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1374376.1374428 |series=STOC '08 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=355–364 |doi=10.1145/1374376.1374428 |isbn=978-1-60558-047-0}}</ref> prove that, in general congestion games, even computing an ''ε''-approximate PNE, for any polynomial-time computable ''ε'', is PLS-complete. Their reduction also implies that computing an ''ε''-approximate equilibrium reachable from a given initial state is PSPACE-complete. They also present ''asymmetric'' congestion with the bounded-jump condition in which, for some states, ''every'' ''ε''-greedy sequence might have exponential length.

Caragiannis, Fanelli, Gravin and Skopalik<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |title=2011 IEEE 52nd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |last2=Fanelli |first2=Angelo |last3=Gravin |first3=Nick |last4=Skopalik |first4=Alexander |date=2011-10-01 |isbn=978-0-7695-4571-4 |pages=532–541 |chapter=Efficient Computation of Approximate Pure Nash Equilibria in Congestion Games |doi=10.1109/FOCS.2011.50 |arxiv=1104.2690 |s2cid=14879292}}</ref> study general congestion games (possibly asymmetric). They present an algorithm that computes a constant-factor approximation PNE. In particular:

* With linear delay functions, the approximation ratio is 2+ε, and the runtime is polynomial in the number of players, the number of resources, and 1/ε.
* When delay functions are degree-''d'' polynomials, the approximation ratio is ''d''<sup>O(''d'')</sup>''.''

Their algorithm identifies a short sequence of best-response moves, that leads to an approximate equilibrium. They also show that, for congestion games with more general delay functions (not bounded-degree polynomial), attaining any polynomial approximation of PNE is PLS-complete.

Del-Pia, Ferris and Michini<ref>{{Citation |last=Del Pia |first=Alberto |title=Totally Unimodular Congestion Games |date=January 2017 |work=Proceedings of the 2017 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) |pages=577–588 |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611974782.37 |access-date=2025-11-25 |series=Proceedings |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |doi=10.1137/1.9781611974782.37 |last2=Ferris |first2=Michael |last3=Michini |first3=Carla|url-access=subscription }}</ref> introduce ''totally-unimodular (TU) CGs,'' where the players’ strategies are binary vectors in polyhedra defined by [[totally unimodular]] constraint matrices. This is a generalization of network CGs. They prove that:

* In symmetric TUCGs, there is a strongly-polytime algorithm for finding a PNE, and for maximizing the social welfare, if the delay functions are convex. The technique can be adapted to matroid CGs.
* In asymmetric TUCGs, in the special cases in which the strategies are matchings, vertex covers, edge covers, or independent sets of a [[bipartite graph]], it is PLS-complete to find a PNE even with linear delays, and welfare maximization is NP-hard even with weakly convex delays.
Harks, Klimm and Peis<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harks |first=Tobias |last2=Klimm |first2=Max |last3=Peis |first3=Britta |date=January 2018 |title=Sensitivity Analysis for Convex Separable Optimization Over Integral Polymatroids |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/16M1107450 |journal=SIAM Journal on Optimization |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=2222–2245 |doi=10.1137/16M1107450 |issn=1052-6234|url-access=subscription }}</ref> present a pseudo-polytime algorithm that computes a PNE for [[polymatroid]] CGs{{Clarify|date=November 2025}} with player-specific delay functions and polynomially-bounded demands.

Even-Dar, Kesselman and Mansour<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last1=Even-Dar |first1=Eyal |title=Automata, Languages and Programming |last2=Kesselman |first2=Alex |last3=Mansour |first3=Yishay |date=2003 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-45061-0 |editor-last=Baeten |editor-first=Jos C. M. |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=2719 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |pages=502–513 |chapter=Convergence Time to Nash Equilibria |doi=10.1007/3-540-45061-0_41 |editor2-last=Lenstra |editor2-first=Jan Karel |editor3-last=Parrow |editor3-first=Joachim |editor4-last=Woeginger |editor4-first=Gerhard J. |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-45061-0_41}}</ref> analyze a [[Optimal job scheduling|job scheduling]] setting where each job is a player. Each job is mapped to a machine. The cost of each job is determined by the load on that machine (all jobs mapped to the same machine have the same cost). Each job in turn moves to a machine that decreases or minimizes its cost (that is, plays a better response or a [[best response]]). They study how much steps are required for the system to converge to a Nash equilibrium. They study scheduling on [[Identical-machines scheduling|Identical machines]], [[Uniform-machines scheduling|uniform machines]] and [[Unrelated-machines scheduling|unrelated machines]]; they also study various policies regarding the sequence of jobs that are allowed to make an improving move.  Their upper bound for the most general case (unrelated machines, general real weights) is <math>\min\left([O(\frac{n}{Km}+1)]^{Km}, m^n\right)</math>, where ''m'' is the number of machines, ''n'' the number of jobs, and ''K'' the number of different weights. On the other extreme, for the case of identical machines, there are policies that converge in at most ''n'' steps, or in O(''n''<sup>2</sup>) steps.

Fabrikant, Jaggard and Schapira<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fabrikant |first1=Alex |last2=Jaggard |first2=Aaron D. |last3=Schapira |first3=Michael |date=2013-07-01 |title=On the Structure of Weakly Acyclic Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00224-013-9457-0 |journal=Theory of Computing Systems |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=107–122 |doi=10.1007/s00224-013-9457-0 |issn=1433-0490|url-access=subscription }}</ref> study '''weakly-acyclic games''' - a generalization of potential games in which, from any starting state, there is a sequence of better-response moves that leads to a PNE, so that natural distributed dynamics cannot enter "inescapable oscillations".

Babichenko and Rubinstein<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Babichenko |first1=Yakov |last2=Rubinstein |first2=Aviad |chapter=Settling the complexity of Nash equilibrium in congestion games |date=2021-06-15 |title=Proceedings of the 53rd Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/3406325.3451039 |series=STOC 2021 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=1426–1437 |doi=10.1145/3406325.3451039 |arxiv=2012.04327 |isbn=978-1-4503-8053-9}}</ref> prove that finding a NE (possibly mixed) in congestion games is equivalent to finding an exponential precision [[Fixed-point computation|fixed point]] of the [[gradient descent]] dynamics of a smooth function, which can be given either by an\ arithmetic circuit or by a degree-5 polynomial. This implies that these problems are complete for the intersection of PPAD and PLS.

=== Generalized congestion games ===
A ''weighted CG'' is a congestion game in which each player may have a different weight, and the delay of a resource is the sum of weights of the players using the resource. A ''player-specific-cost CG'' is a congestion game in which each player has a different delay function. Both these generalized CGs do not necessarily have a potential, and do not necessarily have a PNE.

Dunkel and Schulz<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Dunkel |first1=Juliane |last2=Schulz |first2=Andreas S. |date=November 2008 |title=On the Complexity of Pure-Strategy Nash Equilibria in Congestion and Local-Effect Games |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.1080.0322 |journal=Mathematics of Operations Research |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=851–868 |doi=10.1287/moor.1080.0322 |issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> prove that deciding whether a given network weighted CG has a PNE is strongly NP-hard. This is true even if the flow is splittable (i.e., each player may split his flow among different routes). If the flow is unsplittable, the problem is strongly NP-hard even for a fixed number of players.

Milchtaich<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2015-08-01 |title=Network topology and equilibrium existence in weighted network congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00182-014-0443-9 |journal=International Journal of Game Theory |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=515–541 |doi=10.1007/s00182-014-0443-9 |hdl=10419/95995 |issn=1432-1270 |s2cid=253723798 |url-access=subscription |hdl-access=free}}</ref> proves that deciding whether a given network CG has a PNE is NP-hard even in the following cases:

* ''Weighted'' network CG with two players with ''the same'' delay functions; all players are allowed to use all paths; all delay functions are nonnegative.
* ''Unweighted'' network CG with two players with ''different'' delay functions; all delay functions are nonnegative.

The proof is by reduction from the directed edge-disjoint paths problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fortune |first1=Steven |last2=Hopcroft |first2=John |last3=Wyllie |first3=James |date=1980-02-01 |title=The directed subgraph homeomorphism problem |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=111–121 |doi=10.1016/0304-3975(80)90009-2 |issn=0304-3975 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Fotakis |first1=Dimitris |last2=Kontogiannis |first2=Spyros |last3=Spirakis |first3=Paul |date=2005-12-08 |title=Selfish unsplittable flows |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397505005347 |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |series=Automata, Languages and Programming: Algorithms and Complexity (ICALP-A 2004) |volume=348 |issue=2 |pages=226–239 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2005.09.024 |issn=0304-3975}}</ref> present an algorithm that, in any weighted network CG with linear delay functions, finds a PNE in [[pseudo-polynomial time]] (polynomial in the number of players ''n'' and the sum of players' weights ''W''). Their algorithm is a [[Greedy algorithm|greedy]] [[Best response|best-response]] algorithm: players enter the game in descending order of their weight, and choose a best-response to existing players' strategies.

Panagopoulou and Spirakis<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Panagopoulou |first1=Panagiota N. |last2=Spirakis |first2=Paul G. |date=2007-02-09 |title=Algorithms for pure Nash equilibria in weighted congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1187436.1216584 |journal=ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics |volume=11 |pages=2.7–es |doi=10.1145/1187436.1216584 |issn=1084-6654 |s2cid=17903962 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> show empirical evidence that the algorithm of Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis in fact runs in time polynomial in ''n'' and log ''W''. They also propose an initial strategy-vector that dramatically speeds this algorithm.

Caragiannis, Fanelli, Gravin and Skopalik<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Fanelli |first2=Angelo |last3=Gravin |first3=Nick |last4=Skopalik |first4=Alexander |date=2015-03-27 |title=Approximate Pure Nash Equilibria in Weighted Congestion Games: Existence, Efficient Computation, and Structure |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/2614687 |journal=ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=2:1–2:32 |doi=10.1145/2614687 |issn=2167-8375 |s2cid=5581666 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> present an algorithm that computes a constant-factor approximation PNE in weighted CGs. In particular:

* With linear delay functions, the approximation ratio is <math>\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}+O(\epsilon)</math>, and the runtime is polynomial in the number of players, the number of resources, and 1/ε.
* When delay functions are degree-''d'' polynomials, the approximation ratio is <math>d^{2d + o(d)}</math>''.''

To prove their results, they show that, although weighted CGs may not have a potential function, every weighted CG can be ''approximated'' by a certain potential game. This lets them show that every weighted CG has a (''d''!)-approximate PNE. Their algorithm identifies a short sequence of best-response moves, that leads to such an approximate PNE.

=== Local effect games ===
Dunkel and Schulz<ref name=":15" /> study an extension of CG in which the cost of a player taking an action depends on the number of players choosing either the same action, or a "related" action. They call it a ''local effect game'' (LEG). Their results are:

* Deciding whether a bidirectional LEG admits a PNE is NP-complete. 
* Finding a PNE in a bidirectional LEG with linear structure is PLS-complete.

=== Submodular games ===
A finite game is called '''submodular''' '''if''' (a) the set of feasible joint decisions is a [[sublattice]]; (b) the cost function of each player is [[Submodular set function|submodular]] and has [[antitone]] differences. Topkis<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Topkis |first=Donald M. |date=November 1979 |title=Equilibrium Points in Nonzero-Sum n-Person Submodular Games |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/0317054 |journal=SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization |volume=17 |issue=6 |pages=773–787 |doi=10.1137/0317054 |issn=0363-0129|url-access=subscription }}</ref> proves, using fixed-point arguments, that some submodular games always have a PNE. Two algorithms, corresponding to [[fictitious play]] in dynamic games, generate sequences of feasible joint decisions converging monotonically to a PNE.

=== Concave Games ===
'''Concave games''' (where each player's payoff function is concave in their own strategy) admit efficient computation via [[convex optimization]] techniques.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rosen |first=J. B. |date=1965 |title=Existence and Uniqueness of Equilibrium Points for Concave N-Person Games |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1911749 |journal=Econometrica |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=520–534 |doi=10.2307/1911749 |jstor=1911749 |issn=0012-9682|hdl=2060/19650010164 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Correlated equilibria ==
Correlated equilibria are, in general, computationally easier to find.

Hart and Mas-Collel<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hart |first1=Sergiu |last2=Mas-Colell |first2=Andreu |date=2000 |title=A Simple Adaptive Procedure Leading to Correlated Equilibrium |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1468-0262.00153 |journal=Econometrica |volume=68 |issue=5 |pages=1127–1150 |doi=10.1111/1468-0262.00153 |issn=1468-0262|hdl=10230/525 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> present a dynamic called ‘regret-matching’, in which players depart from their current play with probabilities proportional to regret for not having used other strategies previously. These dynamics converge with probability 1 to the set of correlated equilibria.

[[Christos Papadimitriou|Papadimitriou]] and [[Tim Roughgarden|Roughgarden]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Papadimitriou |first1=Christos H. |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Tim |date=2008-08-06 |title=Computing correlated equilibria in multi-player games |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1379759.1379762 |journal=J. ACM |volume=55 |issue=3 |pages=14:1–14:29 |doi=10.1145/1379759.1379762 |issn=0004-5411|url-access=subscription }}</ref> studied the computational problem of finding a [[correlated equilibrium]] (CE). They presented a polytiime algorithm for finding a CE in various multiplayer games, such as [[Graphical game (game theory)|graphical games]], [[Symmetric game|symmetric (anonymous) games]], [[polymatrix game]]s, [[congestion game]]s, [[scheduling game]]s and [[local effect game]]s.

They also studied the problem of optimizing a linear function of the set of CE. For this problem, they give a polytime algorithm for two cases: symmetric games, and graphical games of bounded [[treewidth]]; and prove NP-hardness for the other classes of games.

Siddharth Barman and [[Katrina Ligett]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barman |first1=Siddharth |last2=Ligett |first2=Katrina |date=2015-11-12 |title=Finding any nontrivial coarse correlated equilibrium is hard |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/2845926.2845929 |journal=ACM SIGecom Exchanges |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=76–79 |doi=10.1145/2845926.2845929|url-access=subscription }}</ref> further studied the question of how to find a "good" CE (a CE with a high social welfare). They proved strong negative results in multiplayer games with succinct representation, it is NP-hard to compute any coarse CE with [[Utilitarian cake-cutting|utilitarian welfare]] strictly better than the worst possible. Similar results hold for CE. Similar results hold also for [[Egalitarian item allocation|egalitarian welfare]] and for [[Pareto efficiency]].

On the positive side, they present a polytime algorithm for computing an approximate CE with near-optimal welfare in [[aggregative game]]s.

== Repeated games ==
In a [[repeated game]], the strategy of each player is a [[finite-state machine]]. Gilboa<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gilboa |first=Itzhak |date=1988-08-01 |title=The complexity of computing best-response automata in repeated games |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531%2888%2990274-8 |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=342–352 |doi=10.1016/0022-0531(88)90274-8 |issn=0022-0531|url-access=subscription }}</ref> studies the following problem: given a game and the FSM-s of some ''n''-1 players, find a [[best response]] FSM for the ''n''-th player. The problem is polytime solvable when ''n'' is fixed, but computationally hard when ''n'' is part of the input.

Littman and Stone<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Littman |first1=Michael L. |last2=Stone |first2=Peter |chapter=A polynomial-time nash equilibrium algorithm for repeated games |date=2003-06-09 |title=Proceedings of the 4th ACM conference on Electronic commerce |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/779928.779935 |series=EC '03 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=48–54 |doi=10.1145/779928.779935 |isbn=978-1-58113-679-1}}</ref> present a polytime algorithm computing NE for an average-payoff [[repeated game]] between two players. Their algorithm relies on the [[Folk theorem (game theory)|folk theorem]]. It computes finite-state equilibrium strategies which can be succinctly represented.

== Related computational problems ==
Besides the problem of computing a NE, other related problems have been studied. [[Itzhak Gilboa|Gilboa]] and Zemel<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Gilboa |first1=Itzhak |last2=Zemel |first2=Eitan |date=1989-03-01 |title=Nash and correlated equilibria: Some complexity considerations |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0899-8256%2889%2990006-7 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=80–93 |doi=10.1016/0899-8256(89)90006-7 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> study the following decision problems:

# Is there a NE in which all players' expected payoff is at least ''r'' (given in the input)? This is NP-hard (NP-complete for 2 players).
# Is there a unique NE? This is NP-hard (CoNP-complete for 2 players).
# Is there a NE in which each player i plays only actions from a subset ''T<sub>i</sub>'' (given in the input)? This is NP-hard (NP-complete for 2 players).
# Is there a NE in which each player i plays all actions from a subset ''T<sub>i</sub>'' (given in the input) with positive probability? This is NP-hard (NP-complete for 2 players).
# Is there a NE in which each player i plays at least ''r'' (given in the input) actions with positive probability? This is NP-hard (NP-complete for 2 players).
# Is there a NE in which each player i plays at most ''r'' (given in the input) actions with positive probability? This is NP-hard (NP-complete for 2 players; NP-hard even for zero-sum games).

For correlated equilibria, problems 1--5 are polytime solvable, whereas problem 6 is still NP-hard even for zero-sum games (NP-complete for any number of players).

Conitzer and Sandholm<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Conitzer |first1=Vincent |last2=Sandholm |first2=Tuomas |date=2008-07-01 |title=New complexity results about Nash equilibria |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825608000936 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |series=Second World Congress of the Game Theory Society |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=621–641 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2008.02.015 |issn=0899-8256}}</ref> prove the following hardness results, even for symmetric games for two players:

* It is NP-hard to approximate some maximization problems on the set of NE;
* It is [[Sharp P|#P]]-hard to count the Nash equilibria;
* It is NP-complete to decide whether a pure-strategy Bayes–Nash equilibrium exists in a Bayesian game;
* It is [[PSPACE-hard]] to decide whether a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium exists in a [[Markov game]].

Bilo and Mavronicolas<ref name=":1" /> study the following decision problems:

* Does there exists a NE where all probabilities are rational numbers? - This problem is NP hard.
* Does there exists a NE where at least one probability is irrational? - This problem is NP hard.
* Is the NE sets of two games equivalent? - This problem is co-NP hard.
* is there a ''Nash reduction'' between two games? - This problem is NP hard.
In a later paper<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bilò |first=V. |last2=Mavronicolas |first2=M. |date=2021-05-29 |title=∃ℝ-complete Decision Problems about (Symmetric) Nash Equilibria in (Symmetric) Multi-player Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/3456758 |journal=ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=1–25 |doi=10.1145/3456758 |issn=2167-8375|url-access=subscription }}</ref> they study a more general decision problem: does a given game nas a NE with certain natural properties? They show, using a general reduction, that most decision problems proved to be NP-complete for two player games, becomes [[Existential theory of the reals|∃<math>\mathbb{R}</math>-complete]] for multiplayer games.

== Concave games ==
A [[concave game]] is a generalization of a normal-form game in which the space of strategy profiles can be an arbitrary [[convex set]] (rather than just a Cartesian product of simplices).

Papadimitriou, Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis and Zampetakis<ref>{{cite arXiv | last1=Papadimitriou | first1=Christos H. | last2=Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis | first2=Emmanouil-Vasileios | last3=Zampetakis | first3=Manolis | title=The Computational Complexity of Multi-player Concave Games and Kakutani Fixed Points | date=2022 | class=cs.CC | eprint=2207.07557 }}</ref> prove that computing an equilibrium in a concave game is [[PPAD-complete]]. In fact, they prove that the problem is in PPAD even for general concave games, and it is PPAD-hard even in the special case of strongly-concave utilities that can be expressed as multivariate polynomials of a constant degree with axis aligned box constraints.

Chernov<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chernov |first=A. V. |date=2019-05-01 |title=On Some Approaches to Find Nash Equilibrium in Concave Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1134/S0005117919050138 |journal=Automation and Remote Control |language=en |volume=80 |issue=5 |pages=964–988 |doi=10.1134/S0005117919050138 |issn=1608-3032|url-access=subscription }}</ref> presents some numeric approaches, related to [[convex optimization]], for computing an equilibrium

== Recent developments and modern approaches ==
=== Machine learning methods ===
'''[[Deep learning]] approaches''' have emerged as promising techniques for large-scale equilibrium computation. Li, Long and Deng<ref>{{Cite conference |conference=International Conference on Learning Representations |last1=Li |first1=Ningyuan |last2=Long |first2=Tianyan |last3=Deng |first3=Xiaotie |date=2024-10-04 |title=Solving Nash Equilibrium Scalably via Deep-Learning-Augmented Iterative Algorithms |url=https://openreview.net/forum?id=NPLty3VT1c }}</ref> introduce the '''Deep Iterative Nash Equilibrium Solver (DINES)''', that integrates deep learning into iterative algorithms, achieving polynomial time complexity by leveraging query-based access to utility functions rather than requiring full utility matrices.

'''[[Reinforcement learning]]''' approaches enabled advances in Nash equilibrium computation. Zhang, Wang, Cui, Zhou, Kakade and Du<ref>{{Citation |last1=Zhang |first1=Natalia |title=Preference-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Data Coverage and Algorithmic Techniques |date=2025-01-09 |arxiv=2409.00717 |last2=Wang |first2=Xinqi |last3=Cui |first3=Qiwen |last4=Zhou |first4=Runlong |last5=Kakade |first5=Sham M. |last6=Du |first6=Simon S.}}</ref> introduce '''Preference-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PbMARL)''', which addresses Nash equilibrium identification from preference-only offline datasets. They show that single-policy coverage—sufficient for single-agent reinforcement learning—is inadequate for multi-agent settings, requiring unilateral dataset coverage conditions.

=== Generative adversarial networks ===
'''[[Generative adversarial network|Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)]]''' are a tool for training models for image identification, by modeling this as a game between the identifier and an adversary. Heusel, Ramsauer, Unterthiner, Nessler and Hochreiter<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Heusel |first1=Martin |last2=Ramsauer |first2=Hubert |last3=Unterthiner |first3=Thomas |last4=Nessler |first4=Bernhard |last5=Hochreiter |first5=Sepp |date=2017 |title=GANs Trained by a Two Time-Scale Update Rule Converge to a Local Nash Equilibrium |class=cs.LG |eprint=1706.08500}}</ref> introduce a '''Two Time-Scale Update Rule (TTUR)'''. Using the theory of [[stochastic approximation]], they prove that it converges to a local Nash equilibrium of the  GAN training game.

=== Blockchain systems ===
Reynouard, Laraki and Gorelkina<ref>{{Citation |last1=Reynouard |first1=Maxime |title=BAR Nash Equilibrium and Application to Blockchain Design |date=2024-01-31 |arxiv=2401.16856 |last2=Laraki |first2=Rida |last3=Gorelkina |first3=Olga}}</ref> apply Nash equilibrium analysis to '''[[Blockchain]] systems''' through '''BAR Nash Equilibrium (BARNE)''' - equilibrium among Byzantine, Altruistic, and Rational agents. This framework addresses the verifier's dilemma in cryptocurrency systems, demonstrating how fines and forced errors can reestablish honest behavior as globally stable equilibria.

== Software and practical implementations ==
=== Computational tools ===
'''[https://www.gambit-project.org/ Gambit]''' is the primary comprehensive software package for game theory computations, supporting both extensive-form and strategic-form games.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Richard D. McKelvey |first=Andrew M. McLennan |date=2006 |title=Gambit: Software Tools for Game Theory |url=https://jmvidal.cse.sc.edu/lib/mckelvey06a.html |access-date=2025-07-27 |website=jmvidal.cse.sc.edu }}. [https://www.gambit-project.org/ Gambit website].</ref> Version 16.0 includes implementations of the [[Lemke-Howson algorithm]], simplicial subdivision methods, and quantal response equilibrium computation, with both GUI and command-line interfaces plus Python integration.

Specialized tools include '''[https://gametheoryexplorer-a68c7.web.app/ Game Theory Explorer] (GTE)''' for web-based small game analysis, and various research implementations focusing on specific algorithms. Integration with modern deep learning frameworks ([[Pyrorchis|PyTorch]], [[TensorFlow]]) enables scalable implementations and GPU acceleration for large-scale problems.

=== Scalability challenges ===
'''Computational scaling''' presents the primary practical limitation, with exponential growth in complexity as games increase in size. Current approaches handle small-to-medium games (up to roughly 100×100 strategies) through approximation algorithms, while larger games require heuristic methods.

'''Numerical stability''' issues arise from degenerate linear systems and floating-point precision limitations in equilibrium computation. Rational arithmetic implementations provide exact computation but at significant computational cost, making ε-equilibria the practical standard for providing robustness to numerical errors.

== Further reading ==
Several chapters of the Algorithmic Game Theory book<ref>{{Cite Algorithmic Game Theory 2007}}</ref> survey topics related to complexity of equilibrium computation.
